title: Fed Credibility Shatters, Options Market Shrugs
dek: The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet the options market prices Fed days like any other—cheap insurance may be an illusion.
why: Sticky inflation, midterm elections, and Fed credibility all point to the same conclusion: volatility is too low, and cheap protection is a mirage. The analysis framework and data are concrete.
who: Fund managers making macro calls, traders watching the Fed's path, and investors using options for event hedging.
skip: If you don't care whether investment content is AI-written, you can skim the last section.

points.h: A Fed without forward guidance is flipping a coin
points.body: The hosts open by noting the shift: at past FOMC meetings, markets knew the odds with high certainty, but this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55-45—barely better than a coin toss. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks about phasing out forward guidance, and every meeting could become 'see the result, then react.' Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage to all assets, so volatility needs repricing. The hosts also assert from history: once truly tested by markets, nearly every official eventually caves, so the current promise of 'never pre-empting market expectations' is itself the variable most worth testing.

points.h: Midterm election volatility is priced like an ordinary day
points.body: Kevin Muir argues that midterm election volatility is severely underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, options priced a ±1.8% one-day move in the S&P on voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it's only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he just spent a prime-time hour talking about 'election fraud,' as if laying groundwork to challenge the result. Muir notes: even if you think he's overreacting, that's fine—as voting day nears, the question of 'will the election be contested' will itself be repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation at historic lows, the odds for long volatility are much better than usual.

points.h: Disinflation is a supply illusion; demand hasn't cooled
points.body: Ahan Manon splits PCE components into 'demand-driven' and 'supply-driven.' Their contributions are now 3.31 vs. 0.38; even if you completely strip out the energy supply shock from Iran, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike quickly and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. The breadth is more troubling: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components are rising faster than 2%. June saw a negative month-over-month print and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but these short-term cooling effects are almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend hasn't been interrupted.

points.h: One hike could have fixed credibility; he didn't do it
points.body: Ben Hunt says Warsh hit a 'self-goal' at the post-July-FOMC press conference. Earlier, the new face and hawkish inflation rhetoric had largely repaired the 'Fed credibility' narrative; but the real move was to hike 25 basis points immediately. Just that one hike would convince markets that 'he means what he says,' and no repeated hikes would be needed. Skipping that step reversed the narrative completely: every independent report in the financial press that week said the same thing in different words—'meet the new boss, same as the old boss.' Credibility, once broken, is hard to glue back; August's gold rally is the market's reaction to 'hawkish talk, no action.'

points.h: After the credibility wound, only jawboning financial repression remains
points.body: Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must manage but cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus fades and tariff pressures return; the insurance sector has a systemic problem with captive insurers being used to take on private investments; and the 10- and 30-year long-end rates cannot be allowed to rise. Any one could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Handling these requires credibility, which was just wounded, so all policy choices are reduced to 'jawboning financial repression'—using statements and intervention to cap yields rather than letting markets price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date; it only accelerates.

points.h: Options market treats Fed meetings like any other day
points.body: Brent Kachuba shows an options term structure with almost no event risk: the 0DTE straddle on the day of Warsh's speech is worth only 38 index points; SPX options expiring August 31 have implied volatility of just 7%, the overall term structure is at 90-day lows, and put open interest is low. He usually avoids trading Fed events because events turn options into a 'tax'—premium is collected before the event, and time value decays once it passes. But this time is special because the market has compressed volatility expectations to near zero and no one is hedging; before Jackson Hole he bought some 'lottery tickets' with very cheap short-dated put spreads, because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't like, naked option sellers will get squeezed instantly. After the event passes, that's a better time to follow directional trends.

points.h: Outsourcing writing to AI outsources thinking too
points.body: The closing topic is Druckenmiller's WSJ op-ed: he publicly said it was written by AI, with the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The hosts argue the key is whether the views and emotions belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual gut judgments, with AI only organizing and expressing, so it's not deception. Ben Hunt draws the line at writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process—'I write to figure out what I think.' When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue: whether the author actually thought through these words. Obvious AI products are already flooding investment blogs; to judge whether an opinion is reliable, don't just look at how polished the prose is—ask whether the view has a thinking process behind it.
